At Tarsel the others stepped into the sun, but I stayed by the window, staring down the valley at that grey fan of stone.
WV13-P01.6.note: The narrator's attention to the railway is all about the bulging wall threatening the track, shown by counting stakes and staying behind to stare at the scree; the line is described neutrally, not criticised, mourned or praised.

If the next winter is like that one, the water will reach the crates under the terrace before anyone can move them, and the pike may be lost after all.
WV13-P02.5.note: The writer frets about the unwalled pool's exposure to flooding (checking the gauge, fearing the crated tiles may be lost) without condemning the choice, which the passage explains by 'Money was short'; 'So the pool has reopened with no wall' read dryly could hint at disapproval, but literally it is a plain statement and the writer never judges the decision wrong.
